Without timely, consistent standards, advanced technologies like hydrogen fuel systems and interconnected energy networks such as microgrids could introduce vulnerabilities before appropriate safeguards are in place. UFC 3-520-05 outlines the technical requirements for the use of Li-ion-based batteries that are stored or charged inside facilities, but it does not address requirements for smaller Li-ion batteries (e.g., in phones and vehicles). Current standards from the Society of Automotive Engineers, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the U.S. Department of Transportation have been established for commercial or consumer applications for some types of batteries, but safety standards are lacking for battery chemistries that are in development or that are not yet widely commercialized, such as solid-state batteries (Beers et al. 2024). Even as standards are established, there can be delays in adoption (Fire and Life Safety Policy Institute 2018), and some stakeholders might adopt bespoke standards or interfaces that are not widely recognized (Sanders and Holderness 2021). The California Public Utilities Commission proposed new standards for the operations and maintenance of battery storage facilities (CPUC 2025) only after improper storage and fire suppression was linked to a consequential facility fire (Pehling 2025). Frequent standards updates through collaboration with civilian partners and broad DOW compliance campaigns could counter this risk. Recent events, such as the 2020 SolarWinds Orion supply chain compromise (CISA 2021), have highlighted inadequate standards for supply chain visibility, which increase uncertainty. The absence of standardized commercial practices for digital bills of materials and software bills of materials hampers DOW’s ability to effectively track suppliers and mitigate risks across critical supply chains (Defense Business Board 2025). Moreover, DOW’s governance structure and supply chain risk management processes face significant limitations in enforcing effective data management and integration, undermining DOW’s ability to achieve comprehensive supply chain visibility (Defense Business Board 2025). Working with vendors to improve transparency and increasing rigor in supply chain management would mitigate this risk. 3.8 Shrinking Legacy Fuel Markets Although advanced energy technologies are projected to act as a stabilizing factor in the global energy market writ large (Su et al. 2025a), their adoption is projected to introduce volatility in fossil fuels markets (IRENA 2024). The International Energy Agency (IEA) predicts a significant decline in global oil demand, dropping from around 100 million barrels per day to 77 million barrels per day, with a 75% reduction forecast by 2050 (IEA 2024c). But industry experts project a more moderate decline of 10–20% by 2040 (Fraser 2025). If the military’s share of the legacy fuel markets grows, such volatility could become increasingly impactful, exacerbating cost swings and the uncertainty of DOW’s ability to find supplies in all deployment locations. More robust stockpiles and long-term contracts could help insulate DOW from price swings in the market. 3.9 Gradual Adoption In the next 20 years, the global adoption of advanced energy technologies might vary greatly across geography and time, requiring the simultaneous use of both legacy and newer energy technologies.
